danish.title: Første epilog (1813–20) — Kapitel 3
paragraphs: Den grundlæggende og væsentlige betydning af de europæiske begivenheder i begyndelsen af det nittende århundrede ligger i folkemassernes bevægelse fra vest mod øst og derefter fra øst mod vest. Begyndelsen på den bevægelse var bevægelsen fra vest mod øst. For at folkene i den vestlige verden kunne foretage den krigeriske march mod øst, som de udførte, var det nødvendigt: (1) at de samledes i en tilstrækkelig stor gruppe, (2) at de forkastede alle etablerede traditioner og vaner, og (3) at de havde en mand i spidsen, der kunne retfærdiggøre de bedragerier, røverier og mord, som ville ledsage den bevægelse.

Og begyndende med Den Franske Revolution blev den gamle, utilstrækkeligt store gruppe ødelagt, ligesom de gamle vaner og traditioner, og trin for trin blev der dannet en gruppe af større omfang med nye skikke og traditioner, og en mand blev frembragt, der ville stå i spidsen for den kommende bevægelse og bære hele ansvaret for det, der skulle ske.

En mand uden overbevisninger, uden vaner, uden traditioner, uden et navn, og ikke engang franskmand, dukker op — ved hvad der synes de mærkværdigste tilfældigheder — midt blandt alle de gærende franske partier, og uden at slutte sig til nogen af dem bæres han frem til en fremtrædende position.

Hans kollegers uvidenhed, hans modstanderes svaghed og ubetydelighed, hans løgnes frækhed og denne mands blændende og selvtillidsfulde begrænsninger hæver ham til leder af hæren. De glimrende egenskaber hos soldaterne i den hær, der blev sendt til Italien, hans modstanderes ulyst til at kæmpe og hans egen barnlige frækhed og selvtillid sikrer ham militær berømmelse. Utallige såkaldte tilfældigheder ledsager ham overalt. Den unåde, han falder i hos de franske herskere, tjener ham til fordel. Hans forsøg på at ændre den kurs, der er udstukket for ham, lykkes ikke: han optages ikke i tjeneste i Rusland, og udnævnelsen til Tyrkiet går heller ikke igennem. Under krigen i Italien er han flere gange sin undergang nær og reddes hver gang på en uventet måde. Af forskellige diplomatiske hensyn dukker de russiske hære – netop de hære, der kunne have ødelagt hans anseelse – først op, da han selv er borte.

Ved sin tilbagevenden fra Italien finder han regeringen i Paris i opløsning, hvor alle, der er en del af den, uundgåeligt udviskes og ødelægges. Og ved et tilfælde frembyder en flugt fra denne farlige situation sig i form af en formålsløs og meningsløs ekspedition til Afrika. Igen ledsager såkaldte tilfældigheder ham. Det uindtagelige Malta overgiver sig uden et skud; hans mest ubesindige dispositioner krones med held. Fjendtlige flåder, der to gange ville have ødelagt hans hær, lader ham passere uhindret. I Afrika begås en hel række ugerningsmandsstykker mod næsten forsvarsløse indbyggere. Og de mænd, der begår disse forbrydelser, og især deres leder, bilder sig ind, at dette er beundringsværdigt, at dette er ære — en pendant til Cæsar og Alexander den Store — og at det er godt.

Dette ideal om ære og storhed — der ikke blot består i at betragte intet af det, man gør, som forkert, men i at være stolt af enhver forbrydelse, man begår, og tilskrive den en ufattelig overnaturlig betydning — dette ideal, bestemt til at vejlede denne mand og hans medhjælpere, havde spillerum til at udvikle sig i Afrika. Hvad han end gør, lykkes det. Pesten rammer ham ikke. Grusomheden i at myrde fanger bebrejdes ham ikke. Hans barnligt hensynsløse, umotiverede og uædle afrejse fra Afrika, hvor han efterlader sine kammerater i ulykke, regnes ham til gode, og igen lader den fjendtlige flåde ham to gange slippe forbi. Beruset af de forbrydelser, han med så stort held har begået, kommer han til Paris. Den republikanske regering er nu nået til det yderste af opløsning. Et år før kunne den opløsning have styrtet ham. Nu kan det kun hæve ham i vejret, at han netop er kommet og står uden for partierne. Selv har han ingen plan, men til sin nye rolle er han ganske parat.
Han havde ingen plan, han var bange for alt, men partierne rev ham til sig og krævede hans medvirken.

Han alene — med sit ideal om ære og storhed udviklet i Italien og Egypten, sin vanvittige selvforherligelse, sin dristighed i forbrydelse og oprigtighed i løgn — han alene kunne retfærdiggøre det, der skulle gøres.

Han er nødvendig for den plads, der venter ham, og så næsten uafhængigt af hans vilje og trods hans ubeslutsomhed, hans mangel på plan og alle hans fejl, drages han ind i en sammensværgelse, der sigter mod at gribe magten, og sammensværgelsen krones med held.

Han presses ind i et møde med den lovgivende forsamling. I panik ønsker han at flygte og anser sig for fortabt. Han foregiver at besvime og siger meningsløse ting, der burde have ødelagt ham. Men de engang stolte og snedige herskere over Frankrig, der mærker, at deres rolle er udspillet, er endnu mere forvirrede end han, og siger ikke de ord, de burde have sagt for at bevare magten og tilintetgøre ham.

Tilfældet, millioner af tilfælde, giver ham magten, og alle mennesker samvirker som efter aftale for at bekræfte den magt. Tilfældet former karakteren hos Frankrigs herskere, som underkaster sig ham; tilfældet former karakteren hos Paul den Første af Rusland, som anerkender hans regering; tilfældet udtænker en sammensværgelse mod ham, som ikke blot ikke skader ham, men befæster hans magt. Tilfældet sender hertug d'Enghien i hans hænder og får ham uventet til at dræbe ham, og det overbeviser derved folkemængden mere end noget andet om, at han har ret, da han har magt. Tilfældet bevirker, at selv om han anstrenger alle kræfter på at udruste en ekspedition mod England, der åbenlyst ville have ødelagt ham, så når den aldrig frem, men vender sig i stedet mod Mack og østrigerne, der overgiver sig uden kamp. Tilfældet og geniet giver ham sejren ved Austerlitz. Og ved et tilfælde anerkender nu alle hans myndighed, den titel, han selv har taget, og hans ideal om storhed og ære, som forekommer dem alle så fortræffeligt og fornuftigt. Det gør ikke blot franskmændene, men hele Europa, skønt de før så på hans forbrydelser med rædsel og afsky. Kun England står udenfor og tager ikke del i det, der nu skal ske.

Som for at tage mål af hinanden og forberede sig til den kommende bevægelse støder de vestlige kræfter mod øst flere gange i 1805, 1806, 1807 og 1809 og vinder i styrke og vokser. I 1811 forener den gruppe af mennesker, der var blevet dannet i Frankrig, sig med folkene i Centraleuropa til én stor gruppe. Sammen med den voksende gruppe vokser den styrke, der retfærdiggør den mand, der står i spidsen for bevægelsen. I den ti år lange forberedelsesperiode, der går forud for den store bevægelse, sluttes der alliancer med alle Europas herskere. Datidens afslørede herskere kan ikke stille noget forståeligt ideal op mod det meningsløse napoleoniske ideal om ære og storhed. Den ene efter den anden kappes de om at fremvise deres ubetydelighed for ham. Preussens konge sender sin kone for at opnå den store mands gunst; Østrigs kejser anser det for en nåde, at denne mand tager hans datter til ægteseng. Paven, folkets vogter af alt helligt, tjener den store mands ophøjelse med religion. Det er mindre Napoleon selv, der forbereder sig på at spille sin rolle, end alle de andre, der forbereder ham på at påtage sig hele ansvaret for det, der sker og skal ske. Han kan ikke tage et skridt, begå en forbrydelse eller øve den mindste svig, uden at det straks bliver til en stor bedrift i de omståendes mund. Den mest passende fest, tyskerne kan udtænke for ham, er en fejring af Jena og Auerstädt. Og det er ikke alene ham, der er stor: det er hans forfædre, hans brødre, hans stedsønner og hans svogre også. Alt bliver gjort for at berøve ham den sidste rest af forstand og berede ham på hans frygtelige rolle. Og da han er parat, er kræfterne det også.

Invasionen skubber mod øst og når sit endelige mål — Moskva. Denne by indtages; den russiske hær lider større tab end de modstående hære havde lidt i de foregående krige fra Austerlitz til Wagram. Men pludselig, i stedet for de tilfælde og det geni, der hidtil så konsekvent havde ledet ham ad en uafbrudt række af succeser mod det fastsatte mål, dukker utallige omvendte tilfælde op — fra forkølelsen i hovedet ved Borodino til frostgraderne og gnisten, der antændte Moskva; og i stedet for geni viser der sig en uset dumhed og fejhed.
Invasionshæren flygter, vender tilbage, flygter igen, og alle tilfælde er nu ikke for, men altid imod Napoleon.

En modbevægelse finder derefter sted fra øst mod vest med en bemærkelsesværdig lighed med den forudgående bevægelse fra vest mod øst. Der er de samme forsøg på fremstød fra øst mod vest — svarende til de modsatrettede bevægelser i 1805, 1807 og 1809 — der går forud for den store vestlige bevægelse; der er den samme sammensmeltning til én stor gruppe, den samme tilslutning fra folkene i midten til bevægelsen, den samme tøven undervejs og den samme acceleration, som slutmålet nærmer sig.

Paris, det endelige mål, nås. Den napoleoniske regering og hær er ødelagt. Napoleon selv har ikke længere nogen betydning; alle hans handlinger er åbenbart ynkelige og usle, men igen sker der en uforklarlig tilfældighed. De allierede hader Napoleon, som de betragter som årsagen til deres lidelser. Berøvet sin magt og styrke, afsløret som oprørsmager og røver, burde han have forekommet dem, som han havde forekommet dem ti år tidligere og et år senere — en lovløs bandit. Men ved en mærkværdig tilfældighed ser ingen dette. Hans rolle er endnu ikke forbi. Den mand, der ti år tidligere og et år senere betragtedes som en lovløs bandit, sendes til en ø to dagsrejser fra Frankrig, der overlades til ham som hans domæne, med vagter og millioner, der udbetales til ham, som om de skulle aflønne ham for en tjeneste.

english.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: The essential fact about the events in Europe at the beginning of the nineteenth century is that masses of Europeans moved from west to east and then from east to west. The first movement was eastward. For the peoples of the West to advance on Moscow, three things were necessary. They had to form a military body strong enough to withstand a collision with the armed body in the East. They had to abandon all their established traditions and customs. And at the head of their armies they needed a man who could justify, to himself and to them, the lies, robberies and murders the movement would require.

And beginning with the French Revolution, the old, inadequately large group was destroyed along with its old customs and traditions. Step by step, a larger group was formed with new customs and traditions, and a man was produced who would stand at the head of that group and of the coming westward-to-eastward movement.

A man without convictions, without habits, without traditions, without a name, and not even a Frenchman emerges—by what seem the strangest coincidences—from the turmoil of French political parties. Without joining any of them, he is carried forward to a prominent position.

His colleagues' incompetence, his opponents' weakness and insignificance, the brazenness of his lies, and his dazzling, self-confident narrow-mindedness raise him to the head of the army. The brilliant quality of the soldiers in the Italian campaign, his opponents' reluctance to fight, and his own childish boldness and self-assurance win him military glory. Countless so-called coincidences accompany him everywhere. The disfavor into which he falls with the rulers of France works in his favor. His attempts to change his career path fail: he isn't accepted into the Russian army, and his appointment to Turkey comes to nothing. During the war in Italy he is several times on the verge of destruction and each time is saved in an unexpected manner. Owing to various diplomatic considerations the Russian armies—just those which might have destroyed his prestige—do not appear upon the scene till he is no longer there.

On his return from Italy he finds the government in Paris dissolving; everyone in it is being inevitably swept aside and destroyed. And by coincidence, an escape from this dangerous position presents itself in the form of a pointless, purposeless expedition to Africa. Again, the same so-called coincidences attend him. The impregnable island of Malta surrenders without a shot; his most reckless orders are crowned with success. The enemy fleet, which later won't let a single boat slip past, now lets an entire army through. In Africa, a series of crimes are committed against the practically defenseless inhabitants. And the men who commit these crimes, especially their leader, convince themselves that this is wonderful, that this is glory, that it resembles Caesar and Alexander the Great, and that it is fine.

This ideal of glory and greatness—which consists not merely in considering nothing you do to be wrong but in taking pride in every crime you commit, attributing to it an incomprehensible supernatural significance—this ideal, destined to guide this man and all who follow him, takes full shape in Africa. Whatever he does succeeds. The plague doesn't touch him. The cruelty of massacring prisoners isn't held against him. His childishly reckless, unprovoked, and ignoble departure from Africa—abandoning his comrades in misfortune—is counted in his favor, and again the enemy fleet twice lets him slip through. When, completely intoxicated by the crimes he has so successfully committed, he arrives in Paris with no plan at all, the dissolution of the Republican government, which could have swept him away a year earlier, has now gone so far that his mere presence there, standing outside any party, can only elevate him.
He had no plan; he was afraid of everything; but the parties seized upon him and demanded his participation.
He alone—with his ideal of glory and greatness forged in Italy and Egypt, his insane self-worship, his boldness in crime and frankness in lying—he alone could justify what had to be done.

He is needed for the role that awaits him, and so—almost against his will, despite his indecision, his lack of a plan, and all his mistakes—he is drawn into a conspiracy to seize power, and the conspiracy succeeds.

He is pushed into a session of the legislature. In a panic, he tries to flee, thinking himself finished. He pretends to faint and says senseless things that should have ruined him. But the once proud and shrewd rulers of France—feeling that their role is played out—are even more confused than he is, and fail to say the words they need to say to maintain their power and destroy him.

Chance—millions of chances—give him power, and all people, as if by common agreement, work to confirm that power. Chance shapes the characters of France's rulers, who submit to him; chance shapes the character of Russia's Paul I, who recognizes his authority; chance produces a plot against him that not only fails to harm him but strengthens his power. Chance throws the Duke of Enghien into his hands and accidentally compels him to kill him, thereby convincing the crowd more effectively than any other means that he has the right to rule, since he possesses the power and the will to use it. Chance arranges it so that though he strains every nerve to prepare an expedition against England—which would certainly have destroyed him—he never carries out that plan, and instead falls upon Mack and the Austrians, who surrender without a battle. Chance and genius give him victory at Austerlitz. By chance everybody now recognizes his authority, his self-appointed title and his ideal of glory and greatness, which seems to them all excellent and reasonable. Not only the French, but all the rest of Europe that once looked on his crimes with horror and loathing—except England, which plays no part in the events to come.

Like probing movements before a battle, the western forces push eastward several times—in 1805, 1806, 1807, and 1809—gathering strength and growing. In 1811, the group of people formed in France fuses into one enormous mass with the peoples of central Europe. As this group grows, the man who stands at its head gains more and more justification for his power. During those ten years of preparation, this man forms connections with all the crowned heads of Europe. The discredited rulers of the world can set no rational ideal against his senseless ideal of greatness and glory. One after another they hurry to show him their own insignificance. The King of Prussia sends his wife to seek the great man's mercy; the Emperor of Austria considers it a favor that this man accepts a daughter of the Caesars into his bed. The Pope, guardian of all that the nations hold sacred, uses religion to promote the great man's power. It is not so much Napoleon who prepares himself for the fulfillment of his role as everyone around him who prepares him for the immense responsibility he is about to bear. There is no act, no crime or petty deception, that he commits which is not immediately reflected in the mouths of those around him as a great deed. The best entertainment the Germans can devise for him is a celebration of Jena and Auerstädt. His ancestors, his brothers, his stepsons and his brothers-in-law are great too. Everything is done to strip him of what reason he has left and prepare him for his terrible part. When he is ready, the forces are ready too.

The invasion pushes east and reaches its ultimate goal—Moscow. The city is taken; the Russian army suffers heavier losses than the enemy had suffered in any previous war from Austerlitz to Wagram. But suddenly, instead of those strokes of chance and genius that had accompanied him so consistently through an unbroken series of successes toward his intended goal, an endless series of reverse chances occurs—from the cold he catches at Borodino to the sparks that set Moscow ablaze. And instead of genius, stupidity and cowardice appear, without parallel.
The invaders flee, turn back, flee again, and now all the chances work not for Napoleon but always against him.

A counter-movement then takes place from east to west, remarkably resembling the earlier movement from west to east. There are preliminary drives from east to west—similar to the probing movements of 1805, 1807, and 1809—before the great westward surge. There is the same fusion of smaller groups into an enormous one; the same rallying of the peoples of central Europe to the movement; the same hesitation midway; and the same increasing velocity as the goal is approached.

Paris, the final destination, is reached. Napoleon's government and army are destroyed. Napoleon himself no longer matters; all his actions are clearly pitiful and contemptible. But once again an inexplicable stroke of chance occurs. The allies detest Napoleon, in whom they see the cause of their suffering. Stripped of power and authority, exposed as a schemer and villain, he should have seemed to them what he had seemed ten years before and would seem a year later—an outlaw beyond the law. But by some strange coincidence, no one sees this. His role is not yet over. The man who ten years earlier, and one year later, was considered a brigand beyond the law is sent to an island two days' sail from France, which is given to him as his personal domain, with guards and millions that are paid to him for some unknown reason.
